claims.text: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy has a single-phase, relatively uniform grain structure.
The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy has limited room-temperature ductility.
Rapid quenching locks in a fine-grained structure.
Controlled sub-critical annealing selectively grows some grains and produces a bimodal grain-size distribution.
Annealing below approximately 80% of the melting temperature is the appropriate sub-critical regime for forming the proposed microstructure.
Controlled cooling rates can balance ultrafine and larger grain populations.
Ultrafine-grained regions increase resistance to dislocation movement and thereby maintain high strength.
Ultrafine-grained regions maintain impact-induced energy-release characteristics.
Larger grains in a heterogeneous microstructure enhance ductility.
Larger grains promote more uniform plastic deformation.
The bimodal microstructure minimizes strain localization.
The proposed treatment significantly improves ductility relative to the untreated baseline.
The proposed treatment significantly improves uniform deformability relative to the untreated baseline.
The proposed treatment causes little to no reduction in strength.
The proposed treatment causes little to no reduction in impact-induced energy release.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys with uniform grain structures typically exhibit strain localization under impact.
Excessive annealing can cause undesirable grain growth that negates the proposed benefits.
Exposure to reactive atmospheres can cause oxidation that negates the proposed benefits.
The magnitude of the ductility improvement and preservation of strength and energy release may depend on alloy composition and processing parameters.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits 'little' strength or energy-release reduction, whereas the falsification rule declares any reduction in either quantity falsifying.
